gap: The calendar section of Rules names the rate card in prose and gives the reader no way to it, and the one route that carries that name lands them on the wrong section while the URL claims otherwise. Measured on the running product at 127.0.0.1:8083 with the shipped dist, Hebrew, signed in as a yield owner: the Rules workspace calendar tab renders one .cal-banner reading 'lekhol eiru'a kayam makhpil timkhur ha-mekhubar le-shikhvat ha-eiru'im BE-AMUD HA-TIMKHUR. ha-shikhva mufelet ka'et...' and .cal-banner-link count is 0. The banner therefore states that a live pricing layer is moving forecast revenue, names the page that controls it, and offers no control, which is the dead-end law. It also names a destination that no longer exists under that name: pricing is now the tab 'kartis ha-ta'arifim' inside the same workspace, so the sentence sends a reader looking for a page that was renamed. The cause is one gate: CalendarEvents.jsx:330 renders the button only when typeof setActiveView === 'function', RulesWorkspace.jsx passes props.setActiveView through, and workspace-router.jsx:230-241 never gives SettingsPanel a setActiveView, so the control is compiled out on every render. Wiring that prop is NOT the fix and would produce a second dead end: measured, from the calendar tab a jump to #Pricing (exactly what setActiveView('Pricing') triggers) rewrote the URL to ?rules=rate_card#Settings while .rules-tab.active stayed 'lu'akh ha-eiru'im' and the rate card never rendered, because RulesWorkspace reads the ?rules query only at mount. The whole fix is inside P5's row and is one pass: hand CalendarEvents the workspace's own open() as an onOpenRateCard callback, render the control unconditionally, name it after the tab it opens rather than 'the Pricing page', and make RulesWorkspace follow a later ?rules change instead of only the one it mounted with. Assert both in tests/test_p5_*: that the banner always renders a control, and that the section follows the query after mount. The Hebrew card is unchanged and still right to left. Ranked behind the named gap, still open: the scope line prints 2391 and 6635 with no thousands separator while the same Today screen prints 8,704 and 50,386 with one; the Today card and the licence page state the same fact in two different sentences (one isolated and locale-directed, one still dir=auto with an unisolated channel name and an extra channel count), so the shared helper this round created is used by only one of its two callers; constraints_restrictions.py stores sentence_en in the notes column and ConstraintBuilder.jsx renders it verbatim; and AiringNights prints '73 min' on one night chip while its eighteen neighbours print a count of airings, so the column cannot be scanned.

bars.bar_2_reference: Ran what I could reach and say plainly what I could not. Linear: reachable, and I read linear.app/docs/sla and linear.app/docs/filters live. Linear's rule register is a strict trigger-then-effect template, 'When Priority is Urgent, add a 24 hour SLA', so every rule in a list parses the same way and no identifier reaches the reader. Meridian's saved restriction reads 'no breaks in the last 8 minutes of <programme> on <date>', which is the same register and the same absence of engine words, and it carries three things Linear's rule row does not: who asked, why, and when it stops. Meridian is ahead on this mechanic. Where Linear is ahead: its rule list is uniform, while Meridian's calendar banner in the same workspace still names a destination in prose with no control, and the constraint builder beside the restrictions list renders a stored English sentence to a Hebrew reader. Stripe: NOT reachable for the mechanic that matters. dashboard.stripe.com/test/coupons/create answers 303 to a login and I have no account, so I could not compare how Stripe states a constraint's effect before saving in its own builder; docs.stripe.com is reachable but documents the API, not the pre-save summary. I did not invent that comparison. Leaning on the stopwatch as the brief directs: Meridian's effect-before-save panel prints two named bases (the plan as saved, and a run of the plan with the rule in it), the money delta on each, the scope the figures were taken over, and an honest refusal with a reason where the second basis is too expensive to compute, which is a stronger pre-save statement than any I have evidence for.
